title: The spirituals
hookLine: enslaved Africans in America made songs of Moses, Jordan and freedom that carried hope and plans

lines: A FIELD BEFORE THE CIVIL WAR.
WHEN ISRAEL WAS IN EGYPT'S LAND.
A BIBLE STORY, OR THEIR STORY?
cards: A field in the American South, before the Civil War. The sun is brutal and the work doesn't stop. Enslaved men and women are often forbidden to read or to gather, and can be sold away from their own children.
Someone starts a song: When Israel was in Egypt's land. Others answer: let my people go. To the overseer on his horse, it might sound like an old Bible story.
To the people singing, it was about them: Pharaoh, and chains, and a God who hears slaves and takes their side. Some of these songs carried hope. Some, people say, carried plans.

teach.b: A spiritual is a religious folk song made by enslaved Africans and their descendants in America. Their makers' names are mostly lost. They grew the way folk songs grow: sung, changed, passed on.
Listen to what they chose: Moses and Pharaoh, the river Jordan, Daniel in the lions' den, the chariot coming for me.
They took the Exodus and put themselves inside it. In the King James Bible, Moses and Aaron go in to Pharaoh and say: "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go."
The spiritual made that line a refrain: "When Israel was in Egypt's land, Let my people go." Nobody needed to spell out who Pharaoh was.
Now, the plans. Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery, wrote that when they sang about reaching Canaan, some of them meant the North.
Harriet Tubman, who led people out of slavery, was called the Moses of her people, and an early biography says she used songs as signals. Historians are careful, though.

Some well-known claims, like songs that were secret maps, are hard to prove, and a few were written down only much later. The songs themselves show faith and resistance at once, with no need to choose.
After the war, in 1871, a small group of students from Fisk University, a new school for freed people, went on tour to save it from debt.
They sang spirituals for audiences who had never heard them sung like that, even for Queen Victoria. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried these songs to the world.

how: Spirituals are sung in many Black churches and in churches of every kind, by choirs and congregations, and are often sung in services remembering freedom, justice and the civil rights movement.

o: any slow hymn sung softly at a church service
a Latin chant that monks sing at evening prayer
a faith song made by enslaved Africans in America

games.q: what's inside the songs — tap the pairs.
p: the one told to let my people go
called the Moses of her people
toured in 1871 to save their school

s: historians know who wrote most spirituals
most have no known author. they grew like folk songs, sung and passed on.
Frederick Douglass wrote that singing of Canaan could mean reaching the North.
historians agree every spiritual was a secret map
some well-known claims are hard to prove. what the songs show is faith and resistance held together.

games.q: it's 1871. your new university for freed people is deep in debt. you're one of a handful of students sent on tour to raise money. what do you sing?
o: the popular songs of the day.
the spirituals your parents sang in slavery.
games.why: the Fisk Jubilee Singers sang spirituals, and they sang for audiences across America and Europe, and the money they raised helped keep the school alive.

practice: Bring to mind one spiritual, even a scrap, Go down, Moses, Swing low, sweet chariot, Wade in the water, Deep river, and hum it if it comes, or just remember its shape.

Think of who first sang it: people with every reason to despair, singing about a God who sets slaves free. If you pray, hold in prayer anyone who is not free today; if you don't, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Spiritual. A song of faith made by enslaved Africans in America, full of Moses, Jordan and freedom.

carryVoice: Your line: let my people go. Exodus first, then theirs. Day one hundred thirty-seven, done.
